title: GPU-Accelerated Multilevel Graph Clustering: A Parallel Perspective on Louvain and Leiden.
abstract: The sequential Louvain and Leiden algorithms are widely used techniques for modularity-optimizing clustering (or community detection) in large graphs. We present pLouvain and pLeiden, two new GPU parallelizations. pLouvain is based on the Louvain+ extension. pLeiden is the first parallel implementation to provably preserve all quality guarantees of sequential Leiden. We achieve this through a novel spanning-tree-based refinement approach. Both pLouvain and pLeiden use a lightweight symmetry-breaking technique that emulates an ordered traversal of vertices. For pLouvain, we develop an alternative iteration strategy to rectify the weak internal cluster connectivity observed in Louvain/Louvain+. Further, both pLouvain and pLeiden optimize the LambdaCC objective function, a generalization of modularity and the related Constant Potts model. On a collection of 57 graphs from 10 families, our results show that pLouvain and pLeiden achieve geometric mean speedups of 3.1x and 8.8x, respectively, over the current fastest open-source parallelizations of Louvain and Leiden. For the clusterings generated, pLouvain yields the highest modularity scores on nearly all tested graphs. The subroutines within these two multilevel approaches could aid in the parallelization of other Louvain-based techniques.

title: Parallel Integer and Learning-Augmented Sorting Algorithms in the Binary-Forking Model.
abstract: We provide parallel algorithms for integer sorting and predictive sorting in the binary-forking model, which is designed to reflect the asynchronous and dynamic nature of modern multi-threaded architectures and languages, where synchronization of threads is accounted for while also allowing for asynchronous memory writes using atomic operations, such as test-and-set. We show how to sort n integers in the range from 0 to n in O(log n) span and O(n) work with overwhelming probability, which is asymptotically optimal and appears to be the first such bounds for the binary-forking model. More importantly, we also provide a parallel learning-augmented sorting algorithm, where a machine-learning model provides a prediction of the rank of each element in the sorted sequence. Given such predictions for n elements in an array, X, we show how to sort X in O(log n) span with work that is proportional to n times the logarithm of the average prediction alignment error of X, with overwhelming probability.

title: Raiders of the Lost Log: Synchronous Parallel In-Place Models and Algorithms.
abstract: Embedded systems and Internet of Things (IoT) applications motivate in-place parallel algorithms, which avoid allocating additional shared memory past the input. Work by Gu, Obeya, and Shun [APOCS '21] defines a family of PIP (parallel in-place) models and parallel algorithms that eschew auxiliary memory at high processor counts while remaining in-situ when run sequentially. However, their models assume asynchronous processing and have no in-place guarantees for intermediate processor counts. We address this gap in the literature by proposing a Synchronous PIP family of models for in-place parallel and distributed computation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our new model by giving efficient and synchronous parallel algorithms in this model that require no auxiliary shared memory and only constant private memory per processor. Importantly, we show how to leverage a new parallel-augmented sweep technique to ensure that Synchronous PIP algorithms remain efficient and strictly in-place at all processor counts.

title: TrioSeq: A Novel Approach to Accelerate Triplet Sequence Alignment on GPUs.
abstract: State-of-the-art multiple sequence alignment (MSA) algorithms are based on progressive approaches that rely on pairwise sequence alignment (PSA) to generate guide trees to align all sequences. Given an evidenced explosion in genomic data availability, research efforts have focused on accelerating PSA on massively-parallel architectures (e.g., GPUs) and specialized hardware (e.g., FPGAs). However, there is increasing evidence that starting from exact 3-way alignments could provide more robust, accurate MSAs, and improve genomic analysis. While the current literature has shown that PSA algorithms can be extended to align sequence triplets, the existent state-of-the-art on hardware acceleration of exact 3-way alignments is still scarce. In particular, current GPU methods are still inefficient due to lacking support for novel hardware features (e.g., cross-thread intrinsics), while being closed-source and vendor-specific. In this paper, TrioSeq is proposed as a fine-grained strategy to efficiently implement 3-way alignments on GPUs, leveraging novel levels of GPU parallelism and synchronization to achieve high throughput in aligning sequence triplets. Evaluation on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs shows that TrioSeq outperforms state-of-the-art GPU progressive methods on 3-way alignment by at least 20% on simulated genomic datasets.

title: Optimizing Multiobjective Genetic Algorithms For High-Order Epistasis Detection.
abstract: One of the current challenges in personalized healthcare is identifying the genetic basis that underlies complex diseases. While Genome-Wide Association Studies have been successful in discovering correlations between Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) and the presence of certain diseases, the study of interactions among SNPs, a phenomenon known as epistasis, is fundamental for a complete understanding of genetic diseases. Epistasis detection constitutes a significant computational challenge, as the sheer number of candidate solutions to analyze increases exponentially with the interaction order, known as the high-order epistasis detection problem. To accelerate the discovery of epistatic interactions, genetic algorithms are often employed as a non-exhaustive method that trades off accuracy by reducing the local search space. However, the quality of the solutions depends on the objective functions, whose optimality for high-order epistasis detection is unknown. In this work, a multiobjective analysis on five well-known objective functions is performed to determine an optimal combination to a wide variety of epistasis models. Furthermore, a parallel implementation of well-known multiobjective genetic algorithms is carried out in SYCL to boost performance and detection power, while being portable to various CPU and GPU architectures. The results show that the combination of four objective functions (Bayesian K2 Score, Gini Index, Mutual Information, and Akaike Information Criterion) is optimal to evaluate different epistasis scenarios, identifying epistatic interactions in 87.47% of all tested models.

title: ViSched: Reinforcement Learning-Based Scheduling for Vision-Language Model Inference on a Heterogeneous GPU Cluster.
abstract: Serving vision-language model (VLM) inference at scale demands scheduling strategies that account for extreme heterogeneity in both model resource requirements and GPU hardware capabilities. We present ViSched, a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) based scheduling framework with dynamic GPU allocation that serves mixed vision workloads— from lightweight detectors on a single GPU to 78B-parameter VLMs spanning up to 8 GPUs—across a heterogeneous GPU cluster. ViSched jointly selects the target node and GPU count for each inference request, adapting tensor parallelism (TP) in real time based on model requirements, service-level agreement (SLA) pressure, and cluster state. On a 100-GPU heterogeneous cluster with AMD Instinct MI300X and MI355X accelerators, ViSched improves SLA satisfaction by 7.3–14.2% and reduces energy consumption by 9.7–17.4% over the best static baseline across three workload scenarios, with the largest gains (+23.4 percentage points (pp)) on VLM workloads.

title: A Persistent-State Dataflow Accelerator for Memory-Bound Linear Attention Decode on FPGA.
abstract: Gated DeltaNet (GDN) is a linear attention mechanism that replaces the growing KV cache with a fixed-size recurrent state. Hybrid LLMs like Qwen3-Next use 75% GDN layers and achieve competitive accuracy to attention-only models. However, at batch-1, GDN decode is memory-bound on GPUs since the full recurrent state must be round-tripped through HBM every token. We show that this bottleneck is architectural, not algorithmic, as all subquadratic sequence models exhibit arithmetic intensities below 1 FLOP/B at decode time, making them more memory-bound than standard Transformers. We present an FPGA accelerator that eliminates this bottleneck by holding the full 2 MB recurrent state persistently in on-chip BRAM, converting the workload from memory-bound to compute-bound. Our design fuses the GDN recurrence into a five-phase pipelined datapath that performs only one read and one write pass over each state matrix per token, exploits Grouped Value Attention for paired-head parallelism, and overlaps preparation, computation, and output storage via dataflow pipelining. We explore four design points on an AMD Alveo U55C using Vitis HLS, varying head-level parallelism from 2 to 16 value-heads per iteration. Our fastest configuration achieves 63 $μ$s per token, 4.5$\times$ faster than the GPU reference on NVIDIA H100 PCIe. Post-implementation power analysis reports 9.96 W on-chip, yielding up to 60$\times$ greater energy efficiency per token decoded.

title: Clust-PSI-PFL: A Population Stability Index Approach for Clustered Non-IID Personalized Federated Learning.
abstract: Federated learning (FL) supports privacy-preserving, decentralized machine learning (ML) model training by keeping data on client devices. However, non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data across clients biases updates and degrades performance. To alleviate these issues, we propose Clust-PSI-PFL, a clustering-based personalized FL framework that uses the Population Stability Index (PSI) to quantify the level of non-IID data. We compute a weighted PSI metric, WPSIL, which we show to be more informative than common non-IID metrics (Hellinger, Jensen–Shannon, and Earth Mover’s distance). Using PSI features, we form distributionally homogeneous groups of clients via K-means++; the number of optimal clusters is chosen by a systematic silhouette-based procedure, typically yielding few clusters with modest overhead. Across six datasets (tabular, image, and text modalities), two partition protocols (Dirichlet with parameter α and Similarity with parameter S), and multiple client sizes, Clust-PSI-PFL delivers up to 18% higher global accuracy than state-of-the-art baselines and markedly improves client fairness by a relative improvement of 37% under severe non-IID data. These results establish PSI-guided clustering as a principled, lightweight mechanism for robust PFL under label skew. Code will be released upon acceptance.

title: Hiding Page Fault Latencies in Graph Processing Applications that Cannot Fit in Memory.
abstract: With graph sizes growing enormously, there is apressing need to efficiently process graphs that cannot fit intoDRAM. The standard solution is synchronous demand paging, which suffers from enormous performance loss as threads idle waiting for data to be brought in from storage. We observe thatt here is sufficient parallelism in graph applications to hide muchof the paging latency, but that the standard approaches suffer from insufficient hardware parallelism to cover storage latencies (symmetric multi-threading) or high software overheads (thread oversubscription). We propose an application/OS co-design where critical page-fault latencies can be hidden by handling in the user-space.The user-space handler issues page-in requests, and instead of blocking, continues working on other parts of the graph while the data is asynchronously paged in. Another approach is to leverage the information in the user space and issue more accurate readahead requests, effectively prefetching more pages to hide future page fault latencies. These approaches significantly reduce paging overhead for many graphs that do not fit in DRAM. To evaluate, we added support to the Linux kernel (+160lines) and ran the GAP benchmark suite in a DRAM-constrained configuration. Our results show that our proposal can hide most of the page fault latency, resulting in a 23% performance improvement over a commodity baseline and 13 percentage point improvement over thread oversubscription. Furthermore, to demonstrate the general applicability of our framework, we also applied it to the GUPS and XSBench benchmarks, achieving 52% and 58% speedups, respectively.

title: DFA-SpTRSV: A Depth-First Asynchronous Algorithm for Sparse Triangular Solver.
abstract: The Sparse Triangular Solver (SpTRSV) is a fundamental computational kernel in scientific applications such as numerical solution of sparse linear systems. However, SpTRSV is very challenging to be efficiently parallelized due to inherent data dependencies. The conventional level-set approach exploits parallelism from the Task Dependency Graph (TDG) of a matrix, and often suffers from high synchronization costs, poor data locality and severe load imbalance. While the state-of-the-art approaches attempt to alleviate these problems through strategies like task aggregation and asynchronous scheduling, they usually optimize SpTRSV based on local dependency and level structures, and thereby lead to suboptimal performance on modern CPUs with increasing cores.This paper proposes DFA-SpTRSV, an efficient shared-memory sparse triangular solver on multi-core CPUs. We first perform a Depth-first Search (DFS) in a top-down manner to traverse the TDG, and aggregate the fine-grained tasks into coarse-grained super-tasks along dependency paths to improve data locality. These super-tasks are then distributed between cores with a greedy load balance algorithm, and asynchronously scheduled for parallel execution with point-to-point synchronizations to maintain dependencies. We present a hierarchical dependency-pruning mechanism to eliminate redundant intra-core and inter-core dependencies, significantly reducing synchronization and scheduling overhead. Extensive evaluation with diverse sparse matrices on x86 and ARM CPUs demonstrates that DFA-SpTRSV significantly outperforms SOTA methods such as SpMP and HDagg, delivering an average speedup of up to 2.98×.

title: ScalSALE: A Scalable MPI+X Benchmark for Lagrangian Hydrodynamics on Heterogeneous Systems.
abstract: HPC platforms are increasingly heterogeneous and communication intensive, yet many commonly used proxy benchmarks either oversimplify distributed behavior or diverge from the structure of full production applications. This paper presents ScalSALE, an open-source MPI-3 based MPI+X benchmark for Lagrangian hydrodynamics that captures key phases and communication patterns of SALE-type workflows while remaining compact and configurable for controlled performance studies. ScalSALE supports MPI+OpenMP execution and includes an OpenMP target offload path for GPU-accelerated nodes (currently for the Lagrangian stage), enabling experiments across homogeneous and heterogeneous systems. We evaluate strong and weak scaling and analyze communication behavior, and we compare ScalSALE against LULESH to contextualize scalability and proxy fidelity. Results show that ScalSALE reproduces the overall scaling envelope of LULESH while exercising a richer MPI communication pattern representative of SALE-style codes. ScalSALE provides a practical vehicle for reproducible scalability analysis and co-design studies on modern HPC systems. The benchmark, as well as the results, are available at: https://github.com/Scientific-Computing-Lab/ScalSALE.

title: Heterogeneous Non-Linear Performance Modeling of Parameter Interactions.
abstract: Important metrics such as execution time and other quantifications of resource usage are not created in isolation. Rather, such metrics pertain to complex non-linear interactions governing behaviors, functions, and operations of myriad parameters. Rather than focusing on a singular metric, we ask: are there hidden insights within metric interactions? Do those interactions hold the keys to new performance insights? If so, where can these parameters be found? What is the method of their identification? What is the process by which the significant parameters may be analyzed?Answers to these questions are nuanced and varied. We propose Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) as one relevant tool for finding solutions to assist modern computer engineers in analyzing platforms at the edge. We show that heterogeneous platforms possess a range of performance capabilities with interesting implications for workloads on such platforms. We show that as workloads run on platforms, workload- and platform-specific factors matter, based not only on the number of execution units but their constitution. Consequently, we propose a means of resource usage identification for modern AI/ML workloads, simulated via GEMM intensive operations, revealing that the interaction of workloads and platforms creates signatures that we explore across a selection of big.LITTLE platforms to identify performance implications.

title: Efficient Communication-Aware Distributed ∆-Stepping for Single-Source Shortest Paths.
abstract: Single-Source Shortest Path (SSSP) is a fundamental kernel in large-scale graph analytics and many scientific and engineering applications, including transportation modeling, network resilience analysis, and graph-based scientific workflows. Among parallel approaches, ∆-Stepping has emerged as a widely used alternative to Dijkstra’s algorithm for handling large weighted graphs. However, existing distributed-memory implementations often face scalability limitations due to frequent frontier exchanges and costly global synchronization.In this paper, we present a communication-efficient distributed ∆-stepping algorithm that eliminates explicit frontier communication. Instead of exchanging frontier sets across processes, our proposed method performs a single distance-only MPI_Allreduce per iteration and reconstructs the active frontier locally by comparing successive distance vectors. By limiting communication to one collective per iteration, this design enables scalable SSSP on distributed-memory systems.Our evaluation across synthetic and real-world networks shows that the proposed algorithm scales efficiently to billions of edges. With 16 MPI processes, we achieve up to a 10× speedup relative to sequential Dijkstra’s algorithm. Crucially, the implementation maintains robust performance across diverse and irregular graph topologies, bridging the gap between theoretical scalability and real-world application.

title: NZFS: A Null File System with Zero-Copy I/O Support for Application Benchmarking.
abstract: As storage technology advances toward multi-hundred GB/s throughput, a critical question emerges for system architects: can applications actually exploit this speed, or are they limited by their own software overhead—system calls, checksumming, protocol processing, and memory copying? Answering this question is essential for extreme-scale HPC systems where checkpoint/restart, in-situ analytics, and data-intensive workflows demand ever-increasing I/O bandwidth. We define the application throughput limit as the maximum throughput achievable when storage overhead is completely eliminated, and present NZFS (Null/Zero File System), a benchmarking file system designed to measure this limit.Existing null file systems such as nullfsvfs enable basic measurement by discarding written data, but they lack support for zero-copy I/O mechanisms (splice, sendfile, copy_file_range) and suffer from scalability limitations on multi-core systems. NZFS addresses these limitations through three mechanisms: discard-on-write to eliminate data copy overhead, null-read to bypass buffer modification, and per-CPU sharding with lazy size commit to eliminate metadata contention.Our evaluation reveals previously unmeasurable application bottlenecks: rsync achieves at most 3.2 GB/s regardless of storage speed, bounded by its checksum computation; sendfile achieves 150 GB/s while splice achieves only 53 GB/s, exposing a 2.8 × overhead difference due to pipe management that becomes a practical bottleneck as storage exceeds 50 GB/s. In multi-threaded scenarios, NZFS achieves 240 GB/s with 32 threads compared to nullfsvfs’s 103 GB/s—a 2.3× improvement due to per-CPU sharding.These measurements enable system architects to predict application behavior on next-generation storage, identify true performance bottlenecks, and prioritize software optimizations before committing to hardware investments.

title: VibeCodeHPC: A Multi LLM Agent System for HPC Code Auto-Tuning.
abstract: In this study, we propose VibeCodeHPC, a multi-agent system based on large language models (LLMs) for the automatic tuning of high-performance computing (HPC) programs on supercomputers. VibeCodeHPC adopts Claude Code as its backend and provides an integrated environment that facilitates program development in supercomputer settings. The system not only brings the Vibe Coding paradigm - program development through natural language interaction with users - to HPC programming, but also enables autonomous performance optimization with minimal user intervention through a sophisticated multi-agent design. To achieve these objectives, VibeCodeHPC implements three core functionalities: (1) configuration capabilities tailored to the unique development environments of supercomputers, (2) collaborative operation among multiple LLM agents with distinct roles - Project Manager (PM), System Engineer (SE), Programmer (PG), and Continuous Deliverer (CD), and (3) long-term autonomous operation through agent activity monitoring and dynamic deployment mechanisms. This paper highlights one of the most powerful features of VibeCodeHPC: fully automated code optimization through autonomous operation without user intervention. Specifically, it demonstrates the performance optimization of CPU-based codes on GPU-equipped systems for matrix multiplication and a Poisson equation solver using Jacobi's iterative method. The results show that the multi-agent configuration employed in VibeCodeHPC enables faster and more reliable development of higher-performance code compared to a single-agent setup.

title: Edge-Native Data-Aware Runtime Systems for Distributed AI: Bridging HPC and Edge Workloads.
abstract: Deploying complex machine learning inference pipelines on edge clusters presents unique challenges: constrained resources, heterogeneous hardware, and significant sensitivity to data movement costs. While general-purpose distributed frameworks like Ray offer flexibility, they often incur excessive overhead for resource-constrained edge environments. This paper presents a novel "edge-native" data-aware runtime system specifically designed for distributed ML inference, applying HPC scheduling concepts to the edge. Our runtime implements locality-aware task scheduling, memory-efficient data management, and a native Rust-based execution engine using the Candle ML framework. We evaluate our approach on a physical 3-node cluster using TCP/IP. Using a batch-processed LeNet-style CNN benchmark, our Rust runtime demonstrates 3.3× faster pipeline execution compared to PyTorch and 62× faster execution compared to Ray. Our system matches the computational throughput of dedicated deep learning frameworks while maintaining a minimal resource footprint (<50MB), addressing the specific constraints of edge deployment. By bridging classical HPC data-locality principles with modern Edge AI requirements, we provide a foundation for high-performance, predictable inference at the edge.

title: CHROMA: High-Quality Robust Graph Coloring on GPUs.
abstract: Graph coloring assigns colors to vertices such that no two adjacent vertices share the same color. As graphs grow in size and complexity, scalable graph coloring becomes increasingly challenging. Although many CUDA-based parallel coloring algorithms have been proposed, they often face a quality–performance trade-off: strict priority orderings can reduce the number of colors but limit parallelism. We present CHROMA, a high-quality, efficient, and robust multi-GPU graph coloring framework that consolidates the smallest-degree-first priority-allocation stages in the Jones–Plassmann (JP) algorithm to reduce synchronization overhead. Building on this foundation, CHROMA introduces three optimizations—efficient loop scanning, smallest-degree calibration, and elastic granularity control—to improve coloring quality, reduce runtime, and provide tunable control over the trade-off. CHROMA further integrates a robust graph partitioning strategy to scale across multiple GPUs. Experiments on diverse real-world graphs show that CHROMA achieves up to a 7× geometric-mean speedup on a single GPU over state-of-the-art methods while maintaining competitive coloring quality. We open-source CHROMA to facilitate future research.

title: Optimizing When, How, and What to Communicate in Shared ML Clusters.
abstract: In multi-tenant DNN training clusters where multiple distributed jobs share network links, communication contention causes severe GPU under-utilization. Temporal variations in inter-job communication patterns make passive scheduling ineffective. We present Proactive Traffic Shaping (PTS), a proactive framework that integrates time-shift scheduling, congestion control, and gradient compression to compactly align inter-job communication, reducing link contention and idle GPU time. We formulate inter-job scheduling as a joint optimization problem and design a dual-synchronous adaptive algorithm for scalability and stability under dynamic network conditions. Experiments on a real GPU cluster with six DNN models show that PTS surpasses Cassini by up to 29% faster average iteration time and 58% lower 99th-percentile delay.

title: FitCache: A Transparent Drop-In Framework for Multi-Tier Caching to Accelerate Distributed Deep Learning Workloads.
abstract: Training in Deep learning (DL) remains highly compute- and data-intensive, with I/O becoming a critical bottleneck as models and datasets scale. Recent studies report that data loading can dominate training time, especially on large-scale HPC systems with shared parallel file systems (PFS). Existing caching approaches either rely on single-tier designs or require intrusive modifications to training pipelines, limiting their portability and effectiveness. In this work, we present FitCache, a transparent drop-in framework for multi-tier caching to accelerate distributed DL training by coordinating fast local memory (e.g., DRAM, Persistent Memory (PMem)) and NVMe as hierarchical caches atop PFS. Our design adapts to hardware diversity, i.e., if NVMe is missing, memory transparently acts as a caching tier, ensuring stable performance. FitCache transparently intercepts I/O requests and issues concurrent fetches across all tiers, returning data from the fastest responder without centralized metadata or static redirection paths. FitCache adapts to dynamic workloads and heterogeneous clusters while maintaining POSIX compatibility. Experiments on Frontier (2048 GPUs) and smaller research clusters show that FitCache reduces training time by up to 40% and per-batch I/O latency by up to 71.6% compared to Lustre Orion PFS, offering a drop-in solution for scalable DL training.

title: Dynamic NUMA-Aware Data Structure Replication.
abstract: Computing infrastructure is increasingly composed of non-uniform memory access (NUMA) architectures, such as machines with multiple sockets and rackscale systems with shared memory. A powerful technique to effectively use such architectures is to replicate data structures across NUMA domains, so threads can quickly access a local replica of data. Unfortunately, existing replication methods support only a static set of replicas, which is mismatched to the dynamic needs of modern systems. We introduce LD-NR, a replication technique that allows the number and location of replicas to change dynamically. LD-NR can adapt to workloads that change over time, such as applications that scale up and down across NUMA domains, whereas NR, the state of the art in NUMA-aware data structure replication, is limited to a static replica set. LD-NR achieves this benefit with negligible memory and performance overhead when configured identically to NR. We show that a hashmap dynamically replicated with LD-NR achieves 2.6 times better throughput than the best performing concurrent hashmap implementation, and provides 97% of the throughput provided by NR with an ideal, static configuration. We further demonstrate the utility of LD-NR to optimize complex systems by using it to enable a granular, per-process page table replication policy in a rackscale operating system.

title: Scalable Spike Transmission in Large-Scale Brain Network Simulations.
abstract: Large-scale simulations of biological neural networks model cells, their connections, and the information they exchange. A key challenge is transmitting this information (in the form of action potentials or spikes) over MPI, which quickly becomes a bottleneck as the network size grows. The traditional strategy of sending all spikes to all ranks simplifies preprocessing but burdens postprocessing, and with more MPI ranks and hardware accelerators, it has become increasingly inefficient. To address this issue, we propose two complementary solutions. First, Targeted Spike Delivery as a generic method that delivers spikes only to their intended receivers through a preprocessing phase, eliminating costly postprocessing and reducing redundant transfers. Being network-independent, it offers a scalable foundation adaptable to multiple simulators. The second solution, called Hierarchical Neighborhood Communication, is a domain-specific method that leverages cell positions and MPI neighborhood communication. By partitioning the network into spatial subdomains, it exploits the fact that neurons mostly connect locally, reducing overhead and further improving scalability while reflecting biological realism. The first approach achieves significant performance gains, with speedups of up to 2.5 in CPU experiments and 6 on GPU, measured on large-scale runs utilizing 10,000 and 3,500 MPI ranks, respectively. When cell positions are available and MPI neighborhood communication is applied, performance improves by a factor of 3.7 compared to the Baseline strategy, complementing the gains of the generic scheme. With these adaptations, simulations are optimized for current architectures and ready to exploit the capabilities of exascale supercomputers. This establishes our approach as an important step toward efficient and scalable brain simulations.

title: FedACT: Concurrent Federated Intelligence across Heterogeneous Data Sources.
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative intelligence across decentralized data source devices in a privacy-preserving way. While substantial research attention has been drawn to optimizing the learning process for an individual task, real-world applications increasingly require multiple machine learning tasks simultaneously training their models across a shared pool of devices. Naively applying single-FL optimization techniques in multi-FL systems results in suboptimal system performance, particularly due to device heterogeneity and resource inefficiency. To address such a critical open challenge, we introduce FedACT, a novel resource heterogeneity-aware device scheduling approach designed to efficiently schedule heterogeneous devices across multiple concurrent FL jobs, with the goal of minimizing their average job completion time (JCT). FedACT dynamically assigns devices to FL jobs based on an alignment scoring mechanism that evaluates the compatibility between available resources of devices and resource demands of jobs. Additionally, it incorporates participation fairness to ensure balanced contributions from devices across jobs, further enhancing the accuracy levels of learned global models. An optimal scheduling plan is formulated in FedACT by prioritizing devices with higher alignment scores, while ensuring fair participation across jobs. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed scheduling algorithm, we carried out comprehensive experiments using diverse FL jobs and benchmark datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that FedACT reduces the average JCT by up to 8.3× and improves model accuracy by up to 44.5%, compared to the state-of-the-art baselines.

title: Control-Flow Execution on CGRAs: A Comprehensive Survey of Architectural and Compilation Techniques.
abstract: Coarse-grained reconfigurable architectures (CGRAs) have gained attention as an architecture that offers an excellent balance between performance and flexibility, making it an attractive platform for accelerating a wide range of applications. Since most practical applications inherently involve control structures such as branches and loops, CGRAs face challenges in handling control flow due to their fundamental nature, and various methods have been proposed to address this issue. This paper focuses on control-flow handling in CGRA-based acceleration and systematically organizes and classifies previously proposed approaches and optimization techniques, providing a comprehensive review.

title: Microbenchmarking NVIDIA's Blackwell Architecture: An in-depth Architectural Analysis.
abstract: As GPU architectures rapidly evolve to meet the growing demands of exascale computing and machine learning, the performance implications of architectural innovations remain poorly understood across diverse workloads. NVIDIA Blackwell (B200) introduces significant architectural advances, including fifth-generation tensor cores, tensor memory (TMEM), a decompression engine (DE), and a dual-chip design; however, systematic methodologies for quantifying these improvements lag behind hardware development cycles. We contribute an open-source microbenchmark suite that provides practical insights into optimizing workloads to fully utilize the rich feature sets of modern GPU architectures. This work enables application developers to make informed architectural decisions and guides future GPU design directions. We study Blackwell GPUs and compare them to the H200 generation with respect to the memory subsystem, tensor core pipeline, and floating-point precisions (FP32, FP16, FP8, FP6, FP4). Our systematic evaluation of dense and sparse GEMM, transformer inference, and training workloads shows that B200 tensor core enhancements achieve 1.85x ResNet-50 and 1.55x GPT-1.3B mixed-precision training throughput, with 32 percent better energy efficiency than H200.

title: Low-Latency Interconnects & HPC Resources: What Does Quantum Computing Really Need?
abstract: High Performance Computing is beginning to play a dominant system-level role in quantum computing for distributed parallel programming, low latency networking, numerical precision, multi-tenant scheduling, and overall resource management. At the same time, state of the art hybrid classical quantum algorithms, error correction, real-time feedback and quantum control impose additional demands on the hardware to maximize system utilization and perform time critical operations. HPC nodes and network architectures are currently optimized for AI workloads. Scaling quantum systems brings distinct requirements and will require us to re-think host system design and interconnects, supported by accelerator co-scheduling to provide fast turnaround, low contention and resource balanced quantum compute.

title: Quantitative Characterization of Host-Initiated CUDA Memory Allocators: Performance, Fragmentation, and Concurrency Trade-offs.
abstract: Modern High-Performance Computing (HPC) and deep learning workloads run on high-capacity GPUs like the NVIDIA H100. As memory capacity scales disproportionately to kernel execution time, memory allocation efficiency becomes a critical bottleneck. While CUDA offers both legacy synchronous allocators and newer stream-ordered asynchronous APIs, their behavior under extreme memory pressure and high-concurrency execution remains unclear. In this paper, we quantitatively characterize host-initiated CUDA memory allocators using directed microbenchmarks. We analyze the limits of allocation latency, memory fragmentation, and concurrency scaling. We show that while the legacy allocator suffers from size-dependent latency, the asynchronous allocator achieves near-constant, microsecond-scale latency. However, this speed comes at a cost. We identify a superblock pinning effect—termed the "Hostage Crisis", where sparse surviving allocations prevent the driver from reclaiming large physical memory blocks. This mechanism leads to Out-Of-Memory (OOM) failures even when user-visible allocations are minimal. Furthermore, we evaluate the performance of per-thread memory pooling under concurrency. We show that user-space concurrency with CUDA pools exhibits non-additive scaling behavior, with throughput degrading as host-level concurrency increases. Even with per-thread pools, throughput is consistent with a global constraint in the driver/OS path, limiting the performance regardless of pool partitioning. Finally, we discuss design trade-offs based on these findings.

title: WaterSplit: Coordinated On-Site and Off-Site Water Allocation For Sustainable Datacenter Cooling.
abstract: Hybrid cooling systems that combine wet and dry cooling have drawn growing attention, as they can leverage ambient air temperature to enable broader regional deployment while mitigating water consumption. However, hybrid cooling remains insufficiently explored because the water associated with power generation is often overlooked. Moreover, distributing water is also challenging when water is scarce. In this paper, we present WaterSplit, a water-aware optimization framework that minimizes the water footprint to enable sustainable datacenter operations with hybrid cooling under limited water budgets.

title: PackKV: Reducing KV Cache Memory Footprint through LLM-Aware Lossy Compression.
abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential across a wide range of practical applications. However, long-context inference remains a significant challenge due to the substantial memory requirements of the KV Cache, which can scale to several gigabytes as sequence length and batch size increase. In this paper, we present PackKV, a generic and efficient KV cache management framework optimized for long-context generation. PackKV introduces novel lossy compression techniques specifically tailored to the characteristics of KV cache data, featuring a careful co-design of compression algorithms and system architecture. Our approach is compatible with the dynamically growing nature of the KV cache while preserving high computational efficiency. Experimental results show that, under the same and minimum accuracy drop as state-of-the-art quantization methods, PackKV achieves, on average, 153.2% higher memory reduction rate for the K cache and 179.6% for the V cache. Furthermore, PackKV delivers extremely high execution throughput, effectively eliminating decompression overhead and even accelerating the matrix-vector multiplication operation. Specifically, PackKV achieves an average throughput improvement of 75.7% for K and 171.7% for V across A100 and RTX Pro 6000 GPUs, compared to cuBLAS matrix-vector multiplication kernels, while demanding less GPU memory bandwidth. title: MeCache: Communication-Efficient Multi-GPU Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network Training.
abstract: Heterogeneous graph neural networks (HGNNs) have exhibited remarkable performance across diverse graph-based applications. However, training HGNNs on massive heterogeneous graphs encounters critical CPU-GPU communication bottlenecks. Specifically, existing systems suffer from: (1) substantial CPU-GPU read overhead resulting from frequent transfers of high-dimensional node features, and (2) prohibitive GPU-CPU write transfer costs caused by updating learnable embeddings for featureless nodes. Caching is commonly adopted to alleviate these bottlenecks. Nevertheless, existing cache-based methods are severely limited by low cache ratios at large data scales and suboptimal designs that fail to address the heterogeneous access patterns inherent in HGNN training.To overcome these limitations, we propose MeCache, a system that mitigates CPU-GPU communication overhead in multi-GPU HGNN training. MeCache introduces two key innovations: (1) a semantic-aware feature reduction strategy that employs type-specific dimensional compression to minimize feature transfer while preserving model accuracy, and (2) a fused caching method that implements differentiated cache structures tailored to distinct data access patterns, along with a cost model for efficient cross-GPU cache allocation. Evaluations on two representative HGNN models and five datasets show that MeCache reduces CPU-GPU communication overhead by 84% on average and achieves an average 2.7× speedup compared to state-of-the-art systems (DGL and Heta), with negligible accuracy loss.

title: Mitigating Artifacts in Pre-quantization Based Scientific Data Compressors with Quantization-aware Interpolation.
abstract: Error-bounded lossy compression has been regarded as a promising way to address the ever-increasing amount of scientific data in today’s high-performance computing systems. Pre-quantization, a critical technique to remove sequential dependency and enable high parallelism, is widely used to design and develop high-throughput error-controlled data compressors. Despite the extremely high throughput of pre-quantization based compressors, they generally suffer from low data quality with medium or large user-specified error bounds. In this paper, we investigate the artifacts generated by pre-quantization based compressors and propose a novel algorithm to mitigate them. Our contributions are fourfold: (1) We carefully characterize the artifacts in pre-quantization based compressors to understand the correlation between the quantization index and compression error; (2) We propose a novel quantization-aware interpolation algorithm to improve the decompressed data; (3) We parallelize our algorithm in both shared-memory and distributed-memory environments to obtain high performance; (4) We evaluate our algorithm and validate it with two leading pre-quantization based compressors using five real-world datasets. Experiments demonstrate that our artifact mitigation algorithm can effectively improve the quality of decompressed data produced by pre-quantization based compressors while maintaining their high compression throughput.

title: A Benchmark Suite for Evaluating Scientific AI Workloads on GPUs.

Currently, most benchmarks lack scientific AI workloads. So, we present DeepKernelBench and the experimental results of evaluating the benchmark suite for early observations and performance comparisons on datacenter GPUs using representative workloads for scientific AI, including Attentions, General matrix multiplications, Geometrics and Fourier neural operations.

title: SkipPar: A Hybrid CPU-GPU Framework for Accelerating LLM Training via Efficient Scheduling of Parameter Updates.
abstract: Heterogeneous CPU-GPU systems present opportunities for hybrid CPU-GPU executions to accommodate and run Large Language Models on limited GPU memory clusters by jointly exploiting the CPU’s large memory and the GPU’s computing capacity. Existing works that employ such hybrid executions schedule compute-intensive operations of forward and backward passes on the GPU and memory intensive operations of parameter updates on the CPU. However, these works fail to utilize the CPU’s compute cycles and characteristics of the deep learning algorithm efficiently, resulting in idling of resources, primarily the GPUs. This paper presents SkipPar, a highly optimized heterogeneous training framework that aims to minimize the parameter update overhead on the CPU that causes GPU idleness. SkipPar is constructed with a dual-stage scheduler to reduce training step times. The first stage exploits the task independence of the parameter updates and selectively "skips" layers for parameter updates on the CPU during the execution of backward pass on the GPU, and schedules the skipped layers in parallel with the subsequent forward pass. In the second stage, we adopt gradient norm-based filtering to filter out insignificant candidates for parameter updates, reducing CPU overhead. We formulate a linear programming model for selecting optimal layer candidates that can be skipped to minimize stalls on the GPU. Our experiments on NVIDIA A100, H100 and H200 GPUs with Llama2 (10B) and GPT2 (9B) models on two large-scale datasets for up to 10000 steps of training and comparing with state-of-art frameworks including ColossalAI, CoTrain and LSP Offload show that SkipPar gives more than a day of saving in training when compared to ColossalAI, up to 7 hours of saving when compared to CoTrain, and up to 17% reduction in training time when compared to LSP Offload.

title: Empowering Scientific Workflows with Federated Agents.
abstract: Agentic systems, in which diverse agents cooperate to tackle challenging problems, are exploding in popularity in the AI community. However, existing agentic frameworks take a relatively narrow view of agents, apply a centralized model, and target conversational, cloud-native applications (e.g., LLM-based AI chatbots). In contrast, scientific applications require myriad agents be deployed and managed across diverse cyberinfrastructure. Here we introduce Academy, a modular and extensible middleware designed to deploy autonomous agents across the federated research ecosystem, including HPC systems, experimental facilities, and data repositories. To meet the demands of scientific computing, Academy supports asynchronous execution, heterogeneous resources, high-throughput data flows, and dynamic resource availability. It provides abstractions for expressing stateful agents, managing inter-agent coordination, and integrating computation with experimental control. We present microbenchmark results that demonstrate high performance and scalability in HPC environments. To explore the breadth of applications that can be supported by agentic workflow designs, we also present case studies in materials discovery, astronomy, decentralized learning, and information extraction in which agents are deployed across diverse HPC systems.

title: A Preliminary Study of LLM Inferencing on Sandboxed Environments for Jetson Edge Platforms.
abstract: LLMs are increasingly used for on-device decision-making in domains such as code assistance, intelligent transportation, and robotics. Recent advances in model compression techniques, including quantization, have begun to reduce the compute and memory constraints of LLMs, enabling multi-billion parameter LLM inference on accelerated edge devices such as Jetson Orin and Thor. As applications deploy LLMs on edge devices, sandboxing their execution becomes increasingly important. In this work, we present a systematic benchmarking of LLM inference on two modern edge platforms, the NVIDIA Jetson Orin AGX and the NVIDIA Jetson Thor, across two sandboxed environments: Docker containers and WebAssembly (WASM), and contrast them with bare-metal execution. We evaluate four state-of-the-art (SOTA) quantized LLMs spanning model sizes from 8B to 70B parameters, including Llama3.1, Gemma3, Qwen32B, and DeepSeek R1-Llama. Our evaluation focuses on key performance and resource overheads of sandboxing relevant to serverless-style edge execution, including inference latency, sensitivity to input sequence length, power and energy, and the performance impact relative to bare-metal execution. Our findings provide early insights for optimizing LLM inference on edge accelerators.

title: Accelerating Clarke and Wright's savings algorithm by multi-threaded parallel processing with SIMD assistance for solving large-scale Euclidean CVRPs.
abstract: Clarke and Wright’s savings algorithm (CW algorithm) is one of the most representative greedy constructive heuristic methods for solving the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP). Given a scenario with N customers, a depot, and a capacity-constraint of delivery vehicles, the CW algorithm initially generates N distinct delivery routes, each connecting a single customer to the depot. It then iteratively merges routes based on the saving values, i.e., distance reductions achieved by merging two distinct routes, under the constraint that the total load of items delivered on the new route does not exceed the vehicle’s capacity. This involves generating ${\mathcal{O}}\left({{N^2}}\right)$ saving values and sorting them in descending order so as to merge the routes with larger saving values preferentially, which incurs the overall time complexity of ${\mathcal{O}}\left({{N^2}\log N}\right)$ in standard implementations, whose execution time rapidly grows for large-scale instances. In this study, we accelerate CW algorithm leveraging its inherent parallelism by multi-threaded parallel processing with SIMD assistance. In our proposed approach, multiple worker threads split up generating the saving values, which is further accelerated by SIMD processing in each worker thread. Following that, each worker thread sorts its own saving values independently, and then a master thread constructs a delivery route set implicitly rearranging the saving values sorted in "thread-local" descending order into "global" descending order to follow the greedy principle of CW algorithm. In order to suppress the rearrangement overhead, it constructs the route set discarding the saving values that become superfluous while the route set construction. Experimental results on a 32-core CPU with Intel AVX/AVX2 SIMD instruction set show that our proposed approach handles large-scale problems involving 30,000 customer nodes in a handful of seconds and achieves 21× speedup at the maximum over sequential execution of a standard CW algorithm on the same platform.

title: Accelerating Sparse-Sparse-Dense Graph Matrix Operator using Asynchronous Execution in GPUs.
abstract: Graph neural networks and transformers are increasingly adopted for learning large-scale, irregular graph data, but their execution is often constrained by high computational inefficiencies on modern parallel throughput hardware. While unstructured pruning has emerged as an effective software optimization, its performance is limited by synchronization overhead and poor parallel hardware utilization. This paper explores architectural optimizations for the Sparse-Sparse-Dense (SSD) matrix operator introduced in MaxK, which is employed during model inference with unstructured model pruning. The inherent synchronization and scheduling bottlenecks fundamentally limit the performance scalability of this operator. To overcome these limitations, a novel asynchronous decoupled execution model is proposed that leverages independent thread scheduling to maximize latency hiding, minimize synchronization and data dependency stalls, and improve the effective hardware utilization. The proposed operator achieves ~50% geometric mean speedup over the state-of-the-art MaxK operator on the NVIDIA H100 GPU and better exploits sparsity for performance.

title: Exploring C++ Standard Parallelism for GPU Programming in a Particle-In-Cell Application.
abstract: In this paper, we evaluate the performance portability of stdpar focusing on the classical Particle-In-Cell (PIC) method on recent NVIDIA (V100, A100, H100 and GH200) and AMD (MI250 and MI300) GPUs. We compare stdpar to established parallel programming models such as Thrust and Kokkos, assessing both runtime performance and ease of use. In our implementation, the method is dominated by the projection operator, which requires atomic operations. Our study includes a first analysis of the performance and portability of atomicity in C++ versus CUDA across different backends. Since stdpar is based on the concept of unified memory, the comparison with other models includes both the version with and without this capability. We demonstrate that while stdpar significantly improves developer productivity, its performance varies with the workload. Notably, on average across NVIDIA architectures, stdpar processes 1.7× fewer particles than Kokkos and 1.1× fewer than Thrust under equivalent conditions. These insights highlight key tradeoffs when adopting stdpar in high-performance GPU applications.

title: FlowSpec: A Flexible and Scalable Simulation Framework for Coarse-Grained Spatial Architectures.
abstract: Emerging spatial and dataflow computing systems increasingly adopt network-connected coarse compute nodes rather than fine-grained lock-step CGRAs (Coarse-Grained Reconfigurable Architectures). However, existing NoC (Network-on-Chip)-based simulation frameworks support either only a fixed architecture or random traffic patterns, irrespective of application mapping, which are inadequate for evaluating and exploring diverse spatial computing architectures. In this paper, we propose FlowSpec, a flexible interface between application mapping and simulation, as well as our FlowSpec-based simulator called FlowSim for rapid exploration of coarse-grained spatial architectures. Unlike existing domain-specific tools, FlowSpec can capture the behavior of diverse computing cores (e.g., systolic arrays, vector processors) and drive accurate system-level architecture simulation via cycle-level simulation of network events. We validate FlowSim against ONNXim, demonstrating high fidelity in performance estimation for neural network workloads while offering the flexibility to evaluate a broader range of dataflow applications. Preliminary results show that FlowSpec can provide a scalable middle-ground for architects, capturing critical system-level bottlenecks and NoC congestion at a fraction of the complexity of full-scale RTL simulation.

title: Reforge: Low-Latency Distributed GNN Serving with Selective Embedding Recomputation.
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been widely adopted for their ability to compute expressive node representations in graph datasets. However, serving GNNs on large graphs is challenging due to the high communication, computation, and memory overheads of constructing and executing computation graphs, which represent information flow across large neighborhoods. Existing approximation techniques in training can mitigate the overheads but, in serving, still lead to high latency and/or accuracy loss. To this end, we propose Reforge, a system that enables low-latency GNN serving for large graphs with minimal accuracy loss through two key ideas. First, Reforge employs selective recomputation of precomputed embeddings, which allows for reusing precomputed computation subgraphs while selectively recomputing a small fraction to minimize accuracy loss. Second, we develop computation graph parallelism, which reduces communication overhead by parallelizing the creation and execution of computation graphs across machines. Our evaluation with large graph datasets and GNN models shows that Reforge significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques.

title: A Minimal and Jitter-Free FPGA Telemetry Core for Cycle-Accurate Determinism in Real-Time Systems.
abstract: This work presents a minimal hardware-only FPGA telemetry core designed for deterministic real-time monitoring. By replacing interrupt-driven software execution with a finite-state-machine pipeline, the architecture achieves a fixed latency of four clock cycles with zero timing jitter. HDL simulation and waveform analysis show a measured internal latency of 20 ns between data-ready assertion and UART transmission start. Implemented on a Xilinx Artix-7 FPGA, the design occupies only 49 LUTs, making it suitable for compact cyber-physical systems where predictable timing is more critical than throughput.

title: Energy-Performance Trade-offs in Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning on SmartNIC-Enabled HPC Systems.
abstract: Federated learning (FL) is increasingly deployed on accelerator-rich high-performance computing (HPC) systems, yet the system-level energy cost of privacy-aware FL remains poorly understood, particularly across heterogeneous networking and server-placement options. We present a measurement-driven study of energy–performance trade-offs for FL on GH200-class nodes across three deployment configurations: CPU-Ethernet, CPU-InfiniBand (RDMA-capable), and a DPU-hosted FL server over InfiniBand using a BlueField-3 SmartNIC/DPU. Using NVIDIA FLARE (NVFLARE), we align node-level power telemetry with per-round timing extracted from NVFLARE logs to quantify time-to-solution (TTS), energy-to-solution (ETS), energy-delay product (EDP), and synchronization behavior for three transformer models (ALBERT, DistilBERT, BERT), trained with and without differential privacy (DP). We find that interconnect choice is the dominant driver of runtime and energy: host-managed InfiniBand consistently reduces communication overhead versus Ethernet, yielding lower TTS/ETS/EDP. In contrast, in our NVFLARE deployment, placing the FL server on the DPU does not consistently match CPU-InfiniBand performance and can be slower—especially for larger models—highlighting that server placement alone is not sufficient to guarantee end-to-end gains. Finally, under our fixed-round protocol, DP increases per-round cost and runtime variance; ETS increases largely in proportion to TTS because average node power remains relatively stable across configurations.

title: OpenSHMEM and Rust: Towards PGAS in Memory-Safe Environments.
abstract: This paper presents a blueprint for the integration of Partitioned Global Address Space programming models in memory-safe languages and provides Rust bindings to the OpenSHMEM API specification, bringing enhanced memory safety to PGAS programming. Through type-level representations of PGAS accesses, our implementation enables compile-time verification of API usage, enhancing memory safety without sacrificing OpenSHMEM’s performance characteristics. Micro-benchmark results demonstrate that these safety measures incur minimal runtime cost compared to direct usage of the original C API, while larger uses show viability in real-world kernels. These bindings enable current programmers to write high-performance, highly parallel programs with stronger safety and correctness guarantees and provide a pathway towards a memory-safe PGAS system.

title: One Memory-Many Paths: Early Experiences with Allocation and Data Copy Strategies on MI300A.
abstract: The convergence of CPU and GPU memory architectures in heterogeneous systems fundamentally reshapes the landscape of High-Performance Computing (HPC) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) workloads. The AMD MI300A represents a significant step forward as the first data center-class Accelerated Processing Unit (APU) featuring a unified HBM3 memory pool accessible by both CPU and GPU, presenting new opportunities to eliminate traditional CPU–GPU data movement bottlenecks. Despite the advantages of shared memory pools, this architectural shift introduces new complexities in selecting optimal memory allocation strategies and data transfer mechanisms. In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive performance evaluation of memory allocation and data transfer methods on the AMD MI300A APU. We systematically characterize bandwidth and latency across a diverse set of memory allocation schemes and data copy implementations, examining performance over a broad range of message sizes and communication scenarios, including intra-APU, inter-APU, and inter-node transfers. Our analysis yields empirical insights to guide efficient data movement on unified-memory architectures and provides actionable guidelines for MPI library developers aiming to design efficient communication runtimes tailored to the MI300A APU architecture. Building on these insights, we develop and demonstrate a memory-aware adaptive prototype scheme that selects data transfer methods based on message size and buffer type. This prototype achieves practical performance improvements in collective communication, realizing up to 60% improvement for Alltoall operations and up to 80% improvement for Allreduce at small message sizes, along with up to 27% gains in real-world application workloads. The results and guidelines presented herein offer valuable direction for leveraging modern APUs to accelerate next-generation HPC and AI systems.

title: Beyond Thread States: Diagnosing Performance Degradation with eBPF and Thread Dynamics.
abstract: Online Data-Intensive applications face performance degradation from load variability and resource interference. While Thread State Analysis (TSA) based approaches enable identifying constrained subsystems, they lack the granularity to reveal the inter-thread dependencies that propagate degradation. In this paper, we present an application-agnostic performance degradation analysis method that extends TSA by capturing fine-grained thread dynamics. We implemented 16 eBPF-based metrics across six kernel subsystems, including scheduling, VFS, networking, futex, multiplexing IO, and block IO which enables tracing thread interactions with specific resources like futexes, sockets, and disks. Our method leverages the fact that performance degradation propagates along inter-thread dependencies, and a subset of thread-resource interactions can enable capturing common degradation patterns. To this end, we employ a selective thread tracking algorithm that traces performance issues from entry-point threads to constrained resources. Experimentation with diverse applications under variable workloads and resource contention shows our method successfully diagnoses CPU, disk, lock, and external service contention with minimal overhead, while also revealing internal application constraints.

title: Where Did My NCCL Calls Go? A Profiler Comparison.
abstract: Deep learning has become an increasingly important technology, with a profound impact on science and society, where modern models need to use several devices for training and inference. Communication among devices plays a crucial role in the performance of distributed deep learning applications, where NCCL is the most frequently used library for GPU-GPU communications. However, performance analysis tools for NCCL still lack maturity, with no clearly established alternative.In this paper, we compare several profiling tools for NCCL based on the accuracy and completeness of the collected data and the overhead introduced. We also introduce a NCCL profiler tool called ncclsee that overcomes the limitations of existing tools. Our experiments with micro-benchmarking and a real-world application show that existing profilers often miss a significant number of communication events, leading to inaccurate results. In contrast, ncclsee records all NCCL calls in every rank, offering more accurate measurements with negligible overhead.

title: Locality-Aware Distributed Allocators for High-Performance Global Data Structures.
abstract: Modern High-Performance Computing (HPC) systems support large-scale analytics but pose challenges for developers in balancing performance and productivity. Existing abstractions, like the Partitioned Global Address Space (PGAS) model, often lack practical mechanisms for improving data locality, which is crucial for performance in distributed systems. We address this issue by introducing the distributed allocator, an abstraction that simplifies allocation and data distribution strategies for distributed containers. Our approach extends the C++ Standard Template Library (STL) allocator to distributed systems, enabling runtime-aware co-location strategies that optimize access patterns and reduce performance bottlenecks caused by remote memory accesses. We implement our solution within the Scalable High-Performance Algorithms and Data Structures (SHAD) library and evaluate it on both an institutional HPC cluster and the Polaris supercomputer. The proposed abstraction consistently improves execution time, achieving an 8.13× speedup (geometric mean) across multiple foundational kernels. Furthermore, strong scaling tests show that these benefits persist across increasing node counts, and in graph analytics workloads, our approach enhances resource utilization, leading to 3.2× higher throughput. These findings highlight the critical role of memory locality in distributed HPC applications and position distributed allocators as a powerful tool for optimizing performance with minimal code changes in large-scale computing environments.

title: Evaluation of Dynamic Vector Bin Packing for Virtual Machine Placement.
abstract: Virtual machine placement is a crucial challenge in cloud computing for efficiently utilizing physical machine resources in data centers. Virtual machine placement can be formulated as a MinUsageTime Dynamic Vector Bin Packing (DVBP) problem, aiming to minimize the total usage time of the physical machines. This paper evaluates state-of-the-art MinUsageTime DVBP algorithms in non-clairvoyant, clairvoyant and learning-augmented online settings, where item durations (virtual machine lifetimes) are unknown, known and predicted, respectively. Besides the algorithms taken from the literature, we also develop several new algorithms or enhancements. Empirical experimentation is carried out with real-world datasets of Microsoft Azure. The insights from the experimental results are discussed to explore the structures of algorithms and promising design elements that work well in practice.

title: Multi-Agent Based Time Critical FaaS Scheduling in Edge-Cloud Continuum.
abstract: Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) platforms are increasingly deployed across heterogeneous edge–cloud environments, where latency-sensitive applications require both low response times and robust scalability. Existing scheduling architectures— centralized, federated, and decentralized—offer different trade-offs between global optimization, wide-area latency, and regional autonomy. However, a single architecture often struggles to fit in dynamic workloads and changing system conditions. This paper proposes an architecture-adaptive, multi-agent scheduling framework for FaaS that can operate under centralized, federated, and decentralized modes and dynamically switch between them at runtime, guided by a QoS-driven evolution mechanism based on long-tail latency signals derived from p95/p50 execution-time ratios. We prototype a framework on OpenFaaS, combining Kubernetes-based cloud deployments with lightweight edge instances on a cloud-hosted edge-cloud testbed. Experimental results show that the dynamic architecture achieves competitive or near-optimal total completion times across workloads, and delivers more stable response-time distributions than purely centralized, federated, or decentralized baselines, while incurring negligible architecture-switching latency and resource overhead.

title: EdgeWeaver: Accelerating IoT Application Development Across Edge-Cloud Continuum.
abstract: The rise of complex, latency-sensitive IoT applications across the Edge–Cloud continuum exposes the limitations of current Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) platforms in seamlessly addressing the complexity, heterogeneity, and intermittent connectivity of Edge-Cloud environments. Developers are left to manage integration and Quality of Service (QoS) enforcement manually, rendering application development complicated and costly. To overcome these limitations, we introduce the EdgeWeaver platform that offers a unified "object" abstraction that is seamlessly distributed across the continuum to encapsulate application logic, state, and QoS. EdgeWeaver automates "class" deployment across edge and cloud by composing established distributed algorithms (e.g., Raft, CRDTs)—enabling developers to declaratively express QoS (e.g., availability and consistency) desires that, in turn, guide internal resource allocation, function placement, and runtime adaptation to fulfill them. We implement a prototype of EdgeWeaver and evaluate it under diverse settings and using human subjects. Results show that EdgeWeaver boosts development productivity by 31%, while declaratively enforcing strong consistency and achieving 9 nines availability, 10,000× higher than the current standard, with negligible performance impact.

title: A Multi-Queue Design for High-Performance GPU Priority Queues.
abstract: The performance of GPU-accelerated graph algorithms hinges on the underlying priority queue. Although there are many CPU implementations, using GPUs to obtain more parallelism is a more tempting and challenging option due to their irregular memory access patterns, load imbalance, and scalability design difficulties. Among these designs, BGPQ is the state-of-the-art method, using a heap-based data structure and batched operations to reach high throughput. However, its design does not fully exploit key GPU architectural features—such as utilizing GPU’s fast shared memory, more flexible warp-level execution, and massive thread-level parallelism.This paper presents MBGPQ, a multi-queue enhanced version of BGPQ. We redesign BGPQ across three axes: execution granularity, memory system, and concurrency architecture. Key innovations include: 1) multiple global queues with random selection to distribute contention while providing approximate priority semantics with bounded rank error; 2) allocating frequently accessed batches and buffers in shared memory to reduce global access; 3) warp-level collaboration to reduce penalty from global I/O. Evaluations on RTX 3080 Ti and A100 GPUs demonstrate that MBGPQ achieves consistent performance improvements across diverse graph datasets. For the SSSP algorithm, our MBGPQ instance delivers an average speedup of 2.37× on the 3080 Ti and 1.95× on the A100 over the original BGPQ. These results validate the effectiveness of our optimization methods.

title: A Two-Tier Secure Event Model for Privacy-Preserving IoT with Encrypted Reductions: A Parametric Feasibility Study.
abstract: Distributed computational models for time-sensitive IoT applications face a critical tradeoff: centralized architectures compromise privacy and are exposed to network tail latencies, while pure peer-to-peer models provide limited support for scalable community-level analytics. To address this, we propose a Two-Tier Secure Event Model that models the edge as stateful autonomous agents and the cloud as a stateless encrypted reduction operator. Tier 1 supports data sovereignty and low-latency local safety actions via append-only logs; Tier 2 performs additive Homomorphic Encryption (HE) reductions over encrypted vectors to enable community analytics without exposing raw data.To assess feasibility under bounded resources, we implement a parametric evaluation harness in Rust. We conduct sensitivity analysis by injecting literature-backed latency budgets for cryptographic operations across a range of constrained edge profiles, while exposing the pipeline to wide-area network (WAN) variability using public HTTPS endpoints. Across 3,000 end-to-end traces (1,000 per profile) collected in discontinuous sessions to capture temporal variance, results indicate sub-second (<1s) latency at P95 under baseline budgets, while conservative profiles reveal a long tail dominated by wide-area variability. Breakdown analysis further shows that WAN jitter, rather than on-device cryptographic overhead, dominates P95 tail latency in our measurement setup, supporting the design choice of local-first auditing to minimize reliance on unstable cloud connectivity.

title: PowerMorph: Shaping LLM Training for Data Center Demand Response.
abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) is driving significant power demand and introducing challenges for the secure operation of power grids. As a result, data centers are increasingly expected to act as active grid participants with obligations to provide demand response capabilities. This has created a need for AI training jobs to adjust their power consumption dynamically based on specific energy requirements. Existing methods are ad hoc, relying heavily on profiling, lacking effective memory optimization and adaptability, and failing to track reference power efficiently. We present PowerMorph, a solution designed to optimize hardware resources and AI training processes to efficiently manage energy consumption during operations. PowerMorph predicts power usage and performance through lightweight selective profiling and interpolation. It makes progressively better decisions, adapts to changing conditions during runtime, and reduces cold starts by analyzing historical data. PowerMorph offers an effective and reliable tracking approach to power demand response curves, ensuring higher throughput while preserving training accuracy. Evaluations on multiple large language models (LLMs), various GPU types, and across varying reference power curves demonstrate that PowerMorph maintains a low tracking error of just 1.8%, achieves up to 197.9% higher throughput, and reduces cold starts by 82.5%, without compromising training accuracy.

title: Evaluating LLM Coding Agents on SZ-Family Lossy Compression Across Architectures.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents are increasingly applied to code translation and optimization, yet their effectiveness in performance-critical high-performance computing (HPC) settings remains poorly characterized. This paper evaluates LLM-based coding workflows on SZ-family error-bounded lossy compression kernels, which combine numerical constraints with memory-intensive and control-flow-heavy implementations. We study two representative CUDA workloads (SZp and SZx) and target two heterogeneous execution platforms: NVIDIA GPUs and Cerebras wafer-scale accelerators. Focusing on single-agent iterative generation, we analyze not only final throughput but also agent runtime behavior, including iteration patterns, sensitivity to prompt specification, and characteristic failure modes. Our results reveal a pronounced cross-architecture divergence. On GPUs, stronger models can achieve substantially higher throughput but exhibit increased sensitivity to prompt precision and optimization guidance, whereas on Cerebras the dominant challenge lies in producing runnable programs under a PE-centric spatial execution model. We further observe that LLM agents are more effective on modular kernels (SZx) than on tightly coupled bit-level pipelines (SZp), where structural dependencies hinder optimization progress. These findings suggest that evaluating LLM coding agents for HPC requires accounting for both performance outcomes and architecture-specific robustness, and that success on thread-based platforms does not directly transfer to spatial accelerators.

title: Achieving Low Latency Inference on High Resolution Images by Exploiting Sparsity in Vision Transformers.
abstract: Transformer based architectures have achieved great success in language, vision, and scientific domains. However, their self-attention mechanism incurs quadratic time and memory complexity, limiting scalability to high-resolution inputs. Structured sparse attention, such as local, global, or region-based masks, has been adopted in vision models like Vision Longformer, RegionViT, and DynamicViT to reduce computational cost. Yet, existing implementations often perform dense query-key multiplication followed by masking, or apply fixed tile sizes regardless of the sparsity layout, resulting in inefficient GPU utilization.We propose a tile-aware sparse attention scheduling framework that bridges algorithmic sparsity and hardware efficiency. Attention masks are represented as binary adjacency matrices and reordered using structure-aware techniques to expose localized dense blocks. These blocks are treated as atomic scheduling units. Offline profiling captures the performance of candidate tile configurations, and an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) formulation assigns optimal tile shapes per block under GPU constraints such as shared memory and arithmetic intensity. Unlike prior methods that use fixed tiling or overcompute within sparse regions, our method aligns computation with the sparsity structure and GPU capabilities. When integrated into representative sparse ViTs, our framework achieves up to 2.1× speedup in end to end latency over FlashAttention with fixed tile sizes, with consistent latency reductions across layers, heads, and attention patterns.

title: Quantifying the Impact of Lossy Compression on Neural Generative Surrogate Modeling.
abstract: Neural networks are used as generative surrogate models for scientific discovery, which are trainable approximations of scientific simulations. These models enable users to replace time-consuming numerical simulations with learned alternatives, providing quick solutions. However, high-fidelity generative surrogate models require massive training datasets, which can create storage and I/O challenges. Lossy compression is a promising way to reduce this burden, but compression errors may affect the model quality in subtle ways, making it challenging to quantify their impact.In this work, we examine how lossy compression of training data impacts the quality of generative surrogate models. We begin by characterizing the uncertainty inherent in training neural networks, showing that identical training configurations can produce different models. By exploiting this variability, we propose a method to estimate how much compression-induced error a surrogate model can tolerate without affecting its accuracy. Evaluation of two application simulations demonstrates that our approach significantly reduces memory/storage requirements and speeds up training while producing high-quality surrogate models. These results show that lossy compression saves data storage up to 23.7× and 39× with negligible impact on the quality of the surrogate model. Meanwhile, reducing the size of the training data set also enhances the data loading speed and reduces the training time by up to 3×.
